articles.title: Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: U.S., China, Russia must draw up a roadmap for talks on nuclear weapons

The first trilateral summit between the Presidents of China, the U.S. and Russia , held in Shenzhen on November 19, reflected both the changing global order and the leaders’ shared desire to remain engaged with one another in an increasingly unpredictable world. For U.S. President Donald Trump, the summit was a platform where he could push for joint talks between the world’s three largest nuclear powers on reducing nuclear warheads. After the New START treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired in February 2026, Moscow had signalled that it was ready for talks, but Mr. Trump wanted to involve China as well. For President Xi Jinping, the summit reinforced China’s position as a peer competitor to the U.S. While Russia seeks to deepen partnership with China, the U.S. is looking to build strategic stability. And for Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the West sought to isolate after he launched the invasion of Ukraine, the summit offered a seat at the high table. The decision to start trilateral talks on nuclear arms and the joint declaration, which stated that ‘a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’, are steps in the right direction. But much will depend on what follows.

Many had compared the meet to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when Russian leader Joseph Stalin, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the future of post-War Europe. But Shenzhen was not a summit of the victors of a major war. This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.

Editorial Context: Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

articles.title: Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India can no longer afford its silence on the multi-trillion dollar AI arms race

The Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Anthropic , PBC is a mile marker in the arms race to develop superintelligent systems driven by generative AI . Traders valued the firm at $1.27 trillion, a denomination that is bound to become more and more familiar in an industry backed by an endless appetite for capital and unprecedented forms of financialisation. Anthropic’s statements emphasise warnings on the safety of its systems and the consequences of unbridled development of advanced systems. In the history of the development of this technology, this PR spin may just be a blip. After all, their testing has led to AI agents that have broken out of sandboxes and infected unsuspecting organisations’ internal systems: a deluge of agentic chaos that is already a reality has led to little signs of the firm backing its words with action. A familiar trend is playing out, with open source LLMs showing frontier capabilities that can back their erratic impulses, appearing in the space of just months, or sometimes weeks. Advocates of pacing the frontier and managing these emerging risks have been marginalised in a way that has little precedent in this century. It is time for governments to get involved, and specifically, for India to raise its voice on these risks, loudly and unequivocally.

While India’s AI industry is nascent, its positions on international forums carry the weight of a sixth of humanity. A mix of cynical calculations and practical considerations have blunted the use of that voice, for example in the U.S.’s hugely destabilising war of choice against Iran, and Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. In taking a strong position on what could be the defining transformation of this decade, India has little to lose, and a lot to contribute. India’s AI policies are geared towards diffusion and research of helpful capabilities that can trickle down to the common citizen. The capabilities that the Union government and State governments seek to boost by leveraging AI are removed from the frontier research wreaking havoc within the information security profession around the world. Out-of-control AI agents promise, moreover, significant disruption to outdated government and private systems online. While India has little commercial leverage to curb San Francisco’s accelerationism, its voice is sure to be noticed. India’s focus on AI in international fora, such as the AI Impact Summit in Delhi, has been on consensus. This approach must change. India cannot be silent amid a U.S.-China technological race which could lead to catastrophic damage. New Delhi must not allow the U.S. to stop it from pushing for AI safety.
Editorial Context: Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

articles.summary: India can no longer afford its silence on the multi-trillion dollar AI arms race
articles.keyPoints:
• India can no longer afford its silence on the multi-trillion dollar AI arms race
• The Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Anthropic , PBC is a mile marker in the arms race to develop superintelligent systems driven by generative AI . Traders valued the firm at $1.27 trillion, a denomination that is bound to become more and more familiar in an industry backed by an endless appetite for capital and unprecedented forms of financialisation. Anthropic’s statements emphasise warnings on the safety of its systems and the consequences of unbridled development of advanced systems. In the history of the development of this technology, this PR spin may just be a blip. After all, their testing has led to AI agents that have broken out of sandboxes and infected unsuspecting organisations’ internal systems: a deluge of agentic chaos that is already a reality has led to little signs of the firm backing its words with action. A familiar trend is playing out, with open source LLMs showing frontier capabilities that can back their erratic impulses, appearing in the space of just months, or sometimes weeks. Advocates of pacing the frontier and managing these emerging risks have been marginalised in a way that has little precedent in this century. It is time for governments to get involved, and specifically, for India to raise its voice on these risks, loudly and unequivocally.
• While India’s AI industry is nascent, its positions on international forums carry the weight of a sixth of humanity. A mix of cynical calculations and practical considerations have blunted the use of that voice, for example in the U.S.’s hugely destabilising war of choice against Iran, and Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. In taking a strong position on what could be the defining transformation of this decade, India has little to lose, and a lot to contribute. India’s AI policies are geared towards diffusion and research of helpful capabilities that can trickle down to the common citizen. The capabilities that the Union government and State governments seek to boost by leveraging AI are removed from the frontier research wreaking havoc within the information security profession around the world. Out-of-control AI agents promise, moreover, significant disruption to outdated government and private systems online. While India has little commercial leverage to curb San Francisco’s accelerationism, its voice is sure to be noticed. India’s focus on AI in international fora, such as the AI Impact Summit in Delhi, has been on consensus. This approach must change. India cannot be silent amid a U.S.-China technological race which could lead to catastrophic damage. New Delhi must not allow the U.S. to stop it from pushing for AI safety.

fullParagraphs: The ECI offers relief to a section of deleted electors but SIR’s flaws remain

Following the Special Summary Revision (SSR) by the Election Commission of India (ECI) in some States that had undergone the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) , mostly in Phases 1 and 2, some 74 lakh names were added onto the electoral rolls. This meant that the electorate in those 13 States, that had shrunk from 49.61 crore to 45.22 crore after the SIR, has now gone up to 45.96 crore. The ECI has extended the SSR to States and UTs in Phase 3. As before, it requires no proof of citizenship or mapping to older rolls, and insists on personal notice before any deletion other than of the dead. It also directs Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) to cross-verify deletions personally wherever they exceed 2% of a polling station’s electors. Draft deletions in Phase 3 of the SIR averaged 17% , and reached 32.8% in Delhi . The ECI also offered another opportunity to electors deleted by the SIR in the seven States and UTs where it is still underway, such as Delhi and Maharashtra, to return to the rolls. Electors who did not return their forms can do so now, explaining the delay, and those who moved within the State can return through the enumeration form with proof of their new address. EROs will process these forms under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and restore the elector’s old EPIC number.

These “corrective” measures follow the Supreme Court’s observation on October 28 that forcing deleted electors to re-enrol through Form 6, meant for new voters, was an “error”. The ECI’s use of remedies that existed in the registration rules is a tacit admission that it went wrong during the SIR. But the measures are limited. They reach roughly 4.5 crore of the 13.37 crore struck off the draft rolls and do not cover electors who moved out of their States. Electors in States where the SIR has concluded, including Bihar and West Bengal, which have already voted on the SIR rolls, can return only through the SSR, by filing Form 6 as new voters, with fresh EPIC numbers and no record that they were ever on the roll. In essence, the structure of the SIR remains intact. Electors must still provide details from “the last SIR”, and those whose details are unavailable or do not match will be asked for documents in a manner that amounts to a citizenship test. The legality of the ludicrous “logical discrepancy” checks remains unaddressed. The 2002-03 special revision offered a better way. Those who had shifted homes were enumerated door to door at their new addresses. The Supreme Court must direct the ECI to return to that model.

articles.title: Talks without peace: On Russia, Ukraine, U.S. talks
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Europe must be part of any settlement on the Ukraine war

The trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. earlier this month failed to produce a major breakthrough or bridge the wide gap between Kyiv and Moscow. Yet, they were a good beginning towards finding a political settlement to Europe’s longest war since the Second World War . In the two-day talks, hosted by the U.S., the warring sides agreed on some humanitarian measures, including prisoner exchange. U.S. representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow after the talks to discuss the proposal. In the next stage, U.S., Ukrainian and European officials will meet in Berlin to discuss a coordinated European and Ukrainian position towards the peace process. As of now, Russian and Ukrainian positions remain far apart. Russia demands Ukraine withdraw from the territories of Donbas it still controls to stop attacks. Russia also wants to introduce limits to Ukrainian military capabilities and Kyiv to declare neutrality (give up its NATO ambitions). Ukraine, on the other hand, has rejected making any territorial concessions for a settlement and asked for security guarantees from the West so that Russia would not attack the country again.

That Ukraine survived Russia’s invasion and continued to resist Russian forces for almost five years is no small feat. But it has also paid a huge price for its resistance. The country has lost more than 20% of its territory. Millions have fled, while men of fighting age are being drafted into the military . Ukraine’s economy is kept afloat by European support, while its military continues to rely on NATO for weapons and other supplies. Until recently, the West stood united in its support for Ukraine against Russia, but that unity has since begun to fray. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, is seeking to reset Washington’s ties with Moscow . European leaders, who initially sought to isolate Russia, have also started reestablishing contacts with the Kremlin. In October, Finnish and Norwegian leaders held direct talks with Mr. Putin. To be sure, Ukraine’s long-range strikes can hurt Russia, as the recent attack on the Kerch Bridge demonstrated. But such strikes are unlikely to change the Kremlin’s thinking about the war. As the conflict drags on, Ukraine’s position is weakening, and its allies are growing increasingly divided. After almost five years, Russia has failed to take a decisive victory. Ukraine does not have a credible path towards victory either. A diplomatic settlement, therefore, is the only way forward. The Abu Dhabi talks recognised this reality. But for the process to be meaningful, Europe must also be brought to the negotiating table.

articles.summary: Europe must be part of any settlement on the Ukraine war
articles.keyPoints:
• Europe must be part of any settlement on the Ukraine war
• The trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. earlier this month failed to produce a major breakthrough or bridge the wide gap between Kyiv and Moscow. Yet, they were a good beginning towards finding a political settlement to Europe’s longest war since the Second World War . In the two-day talks, hosted by the U.S., the warring sides agreed on some humanitarian measures, including prisoner exchange. U.S. representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow after the talks to discuss the proposal. In the next stage, U.S., Ukrainian and European officials will meet in Berlin to discuss a coordinated European and Ukrainian position towards the peace process. As of now, Russian and Ukrainian positions remain far apart. Russia demands Ukraine withdraw from the territories of Donbas it still controls to stop attacks. Russia also wants to introduce limits to Ukrainian military capabilities and Kyiv to declare neutrality (give up its NATO ambitions). Ukraine, on the other hand, has rejected making any territorial concessions for a settlement and asked for security guarantees from the West so that Russia would not attack the country again.
• That Ukraine survived Russia’s invasion and continued to resist Russian forces for almost five years is no small feat. But it has also paid a huge price for its resistance. The country has lost more than 20% of its territory. Millions have fled, while men of fighting age are being drafted into the military . Ukraine’s economy is kept afloat by European support, while its military continues to rely on NATO for weapons and other supplies. Until recently, the West stood united in its support for Ukraine against Russia, but that unity has since begun to fray. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, is seeking to reset Washington’s ties with Moscow . European leaders, who initially sought to isolate Russia, have also started reestablishing contacts with the Kremlin. In October, Finnish and Norwegian leaders held direct talks with Mr. Putin. To be sure, Ukraine’s long-range strikes can hurt Russia, as the recent attack on the Kerch Bridge demonstrated. But such strikes are unlikely to change the Kremlin’s thinking about the war. As the conflict drags on, Ukraine’s position is weakening, and its allies are growing increasingly divided. After almost five years, Russia has failed to take a decisive victory. Ukraine does not have a credible path towards victory either. A diplomatic settlement, therefore, is the only way forward. The Abu Dhabi talks recognised this reality. But for the process to be meaningful, Europe must also be brought to the negotiating table.

fullParagraphs: India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand

New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.

For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.

articles.title: Many imperatives: On India’s Asia diplomacy
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India must shore up its partnerships in the Asian region

Each year, the summits of the 11-member Association of South-East Asian Nations mark an important moment on the diplomatic calendar: India is able to interact with all of its partners in the Indo-Pacific and engage global powers at the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s talks with Indo-Pacific players focused on a future shaped “not by competition, but by cooperation”. This year, the summit in Manila hosted by the Philippines had many other imperatives. These were the first ASEAN summits since the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran and Iran’s Hormuz blockade and strikes on Gulf countries that have upended energy and trade across South and South East Asia. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for “peace, stability, and predictability” in the world during the EAS was aimed as much at leaders from the U.S., Russia and China as it was for the region. The visit had a bilateral context — the Philippines and India have intensified ties considerably in the past year, since the visit of President Bongbong Marcos to Delhi in August 2025, including the upgradation of the Strategic Partnership, maritime exchanges and negotiations over the supply of more Indian-made Brahmos missile battery systems to the Philippines. This year, after months of concerns about U.S. President Donald Trump’s lack of interest in the Quad grouping, the U.S. decided to host a summit of U.S.-India-Australia-Japan Quad leaders on the side-lines of the ASEAN summits, the first time the summit has been held in a non-Quad country.

Given the stakes, there were several outcomes from all the three summits that PM Modi attended back-to-back on Tuesday — the ASEAN India Summit launched a new cooperation on disaster management, and the East Asia Summit focused on countering cyber-crime. PM Modi’s announcement that India would give all ASEAN citizens free tourist visas is expected to increase people-to-people interactions and trade. At the Quad summit, President Trump made a number of announcements including the launch of a Quad Business leaders forum, to be held in Mumbai next year, and the first Quad naval exercises with patrol aircraft. However, the outcomes in Manila paled in significance to the anticipation over Mr. Trump’s next stop in Shenzhen for the Asia Pacific Economic Conference (APEC), with an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping planned on Thursday. New Delhi must watch the outcomes of that summit among the “global superpowers” much more closely.

articles.title: Andhra Pradesh gets national recognition for its progress in HIV/AIDS control
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Six districts in the State have achieved ‘Surakshit’ status and another 10 the ‘Saksham’ status, and the rankings are based on a district’s performance on 95-95-95 targets fixed by the Joint United Nations Programme
Andhra Pradesh has received national recognition for its progress in controlling HIV, with six districts in the State achieving the ‘Surakshit’ status and another 10 achieving the ‘Saksham’ status.

According to a release from the department, the districts of Chittoor, East Godavari, Guntur, Kakinada, Visakhapatnam and Vizianagaram achieved ‘Surakshit’ status, while the districts of Anakapalli, Anantapur, Bapatla, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, Eluru, Kurnool, Parvathipuram-Manyam, Srikakulam, Tirupati and YSR Kadapa achieved the ‘Saksham’ status.
The rankings are based on a district’s performance on 95-95-95 targets, fixed by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS(UNAIDS) as part of efforts to end the epidemic by 2030.

The three targets include ensuring that 95% of people living with HIV know their status, providing antiretroviral therapy (ART) to 95% of those diagnosed; and achieving viral suppression in 95% of those receiving treatment.

According to the release, the percentage of people living with HIV who knew their status increased from 87.7% in April 2026 to 92.7% in October, and currently stands at 92.8%. Between April and October, 7,641 new HIV cases were identified through Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres.
The number of people receiving ART increased from 2,41,507 in April to 2,65,690 in October, an additional 24,183 patients. Viral suppression has been achieved in 96.4% of those undergoing treatment.
Reacting to the development, Minister for Health, Medical and Family Welfare Satya Kumar Yadav said 16 districts improved their performance between April and October.

The release stated that the A.P. State AIDS Control Society (APSACS) developed ‘Suraksha’ portal to monitor HIV testing, diagnosis and treatment services. It also launched ‘Each One Reach One’ initiative, to bring patients who had discontinued medication back into treatment. These two measures also helped the State achieve the targets.
Mr. Satya Kumar said priority was to ensure timely diagnosis, continuous treatment and quality healthcare without discrimination for everyone living with HIV.
APSACS Project Director Smaran Raj said the organisation was committed to bringing three more districts to ‘Surakshit’ status in the week.

articles.title: 14-year-old used AI chatbot to hack Agniveer ‘test’ website, wanted to earn money by selling it on dark web: Delhi police sources
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Haryana teenager used an AI chatbot to identify valuable data and find a way into the test portal; preliminary investigation suggests only names and addresses were accessed, Delhi Police sources say

A 14-year-old boy from Haryana’s Ballabhgarh, who was apprehended for attempting to sell sensitive information linked to around 4,000 Agniveer personnel on the dark web, used artificial intelligence tools to “identify data that could fetch him money and sought the chatbot’s help to hack into a website”, a senior official familiar with the investigation told The Hindu .
The boy gained unauthorised access to a test website designed for former Agniveers to register themselves and explore employment opportunities in the Indian Armed Forces.

“Preliminary investigation has revealed that the boy managed to breach only the test website, gaining access to names and addresses. There is no indication so far that information relating to marks, ranks, results or other sensitive personnel records was compromised,” the official said.
During preliminary questioning, the boy told investigators that he was motivated by the prospect of making money.

“He said he first asked an AI chatbot to identify what kind of data could help him earn money. He then sought its assistance in finding a way to hack into the system and access such information,” the official said. The exact method used to gain access to the website is still being examined.

After accessing the website, the boy allegedly extracted the information and advertised it on a dark web marketplace, claiming to possess personal records of around 4,000 Agniveer personnel and sought $500 for the purported database.

The Delhi Police’s Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit has recovered data from the juvenile’s digital devices. Investigators are now examining the material to establish its authenticity and determine the extent of the suspected breach.

The IFSO unit has also written to the National Informatics Centre (NIC), seeking clarification on the data available on the test website and the information accessed by the boy. The police are awaiting a response to ascertain precisely what information may have been compromised.

While the NIC provides digital infrastructure and hosts government portals, the ownership and maintenance of Agniveer personnel records rest with the Armed Forces and the concerned ministries, officials said.
As the accused is a juvenile, he was counselled and handed over to his parents. The police are consulting the Juvenile Justice Board on the further course of action.

articles.title: T.N. may see solar energy installations slowing down, say energy generators
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: In the last one month, some of the solar energy generators received notices demanding 8% banking charges.
Tamil Nadu, which has 10,000 MW-11,000 MW of installed solar energy capacity, may see a slowdown in solar energy installations in 2027, according to industry representatives.

The single window system for obtaining approvals is not functioning effectively, finer details based on the recently-announced Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Policy should be notified by the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission, and costs are escalating, say solar energy investors.

“No approvals have been granted for solar energy projects for almost six months now. Only now has the government started accepting the applications. Even if they are approved now, it is difficult to commission the projects by March 2027. From April next year, it is mandatory for all new projects to have BESS, and this will push the costs up,” said one of the solar energy investors in Coimbatore.

“We had a detailed discussion with the TNERC on the BESS policy. The policy says there will be waiver of wheeling charges. The wheeling charges are applicable only if a consumer buys under open access. However, the policy says solar energy generators who store energy can sell it only to the State utility. There are many such issues with the policy that need better clarity in the policy ,” says AD Thirumoorthy, State Level Renewable Energy Committee Member, Government of Tamil Nadu.

The single window approval system is functioning effectively for solar energy projects that come as a part of foreign direct investments. The others require multiple approvals, starting right from the rural local body heads. These lead to delays, pushing up the costs, he added.

While the BESS policy is a welcome move, the Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation should ensure that stored solar energy is evacuated within 24 hours, so that the generator can store freshly generated energy the next day, said L. Santhosh, president of the Tamil Nadu Electricity Consumers Association.

In the last one month, some of the solar energy generators received notices demanding 8% banking charges. These are not applicable because the court has stayed the green energy open access policy of the State, he added. More sub-stations and solutions for right of way challenges to lay lines on lands belonging to various government departments are among the other issues faced by investors that threaten to slow down solar energy projects.

articles.title: Three cyclones in three weeks: What’s happening in the Bay of Bengal? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Such a frequency is uncommon but not unique this year; there were around 1.8 cyclones a year in the post-monsoon period in 1982-2022, with the average increasing after 2001

The story so far: Within 23 days this year, three cyclones formed over the Bay of Bengal. Of them, Cyclone Arnab made landfall near Yanam on the Andhra Pradesh coast on October 28 and Murasu on November 3 near Ongole. Cyclone Akvan formed on November 16 and made landfall near Gopalpur in Odisha on Friday morning (November 20, 2026).

A cyclone requires an atmospheric disturbance, abundant moisture, and favourable winds. The Bay has two main cyclone seasons, April-May and October-December. During the southwest monsoon, strong winds blowing in different directions at different altitudes suppress cyclone formation. But as the monsoon withdraws, the vertical wind shear weakens even as the waters remain warm, creating more favourable conditions.

articles.title: FUJIFILM’s Spectrum tour enthrals visual creators, photography enthusiasts in Bengaluru
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The three-day event featured specialised experience zones focusing on distinct creative mediums, including vlogging, cinematography, street photography and portraiture
A multi-city FUJIFILM India Spectrum Tour, bringing together of the brand’s entire range of imaging solutions from Instax cameras, digital cameras and lenses, concluded in Bengaluru recently.

The three-day event, held at the Venkatappa Art Gallery, featured specialised experience zones focusing on distinct creative mediums, including vlogging, cinematography, street photography and portraiture, attracted a large number of people.

Company executives highlighted the regional strategy behind selecting the city for this segment of the tour. "We are excited to connect with the city’s vibrant imaging community. Through Spectrum, we aim to bring our imaging heritage and cutting-edge technology closer to creators,"’ said Koji Wada, managing director of FUJIFILM India.

The tour was in Bengaluru after Gurugram and Ahmedabad, attracting local photography enthusiasts, visual creators and students who prefer to have a hands-on experience with FUJIFILM product ranges. A central component involved educational masterclasses led by established industry practitioners. Photographers including Sudhir Ramachandran and Prashant Godbole were among the participants.

Sessions covered architectural, landscape, and street photography. Other sessions led by technical experts covered niche genres such as astrophotography, wildlife documentation, and sports imaging. The event consolidated the company’s various product categories, including mirrorless camera systems, instant photography devices, and optical tools, under a unified interactive environment.

Arun Babu, associate director of the Imaging Solutions Division at FUJIFILM India, said, “In Bengaluru, through hands-on experiences, we encouraged visitors to experiment with our imaging solutions and discover new ways to express their creativity.”

Sessions covered architectural, landscape, and street photography. Other sessions led by technical experts covered niche genres such as astrophotography, wildlife documentation, and sports imaging. The event consolidated the company’s various product categories, including mirrorless camera systems, instant photography devices, and optical tools, under a unified interactive environment.

articles.title: Kashmir’s famed saffron fields have been used as dumping grounds for three years: Mehbooba Mufti
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The former Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister says nearly 2,000 kanals of land have been damaged, threatening the livelihoods of 150 families; the NGT has directed a panel to inspect the site and recommend action

Kashmir’s prized saffron fields in Pampore, Pulwama, have been used as a municipal dumping ground for the past three years, former Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister and Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) president Mehbooba Mufti said on Saturday (November 21, 2026).

“For the past three years, Pampore’s priceless saffron fields have been used as a municipal dumping ground. Nearly 2,000 kanals were damaged, 150 families’ livelihoods threatened, and rats and rodents destroying crops. This is an outrageous assault on Kashmir’s saffron heritage. Such administrative negligence is indefensible. Our saffron fields are not dumping sites. They must be protected not poisoned,” Ms. Mufti said.

Her statement came days after the National Green Tribunal (NGT) highlighted the “unscientific dumping of municipal solid waste in Patalbagh” in Pampore. The NGT bench, comprising chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and expert member Dr. Afroz Alam, directed the constitution of a joint committee “to conduct an on-site inspection and submit a comprehensive factual and action-taken report within eight weeks”.

It asked the Deputy Commissioner, Pulwama, to coordinate the inspection and facilitate the committee’s visit to the dumping site. Representatives of the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir (SKUAST-K), the Regional Director of the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and a nominee of the Member Secretary, Jammu and Kashmir Pollution Control Committee, will be members of the committee.

The committee will examine the extent of pollution caused by the waste dumping, assess its impact on saffron cultivation spread over approximately 2,000 kanals of land and adjoining areas, and ascertain whether the dumping site has obtained the requisite statutory clearances, officials said

articles.title: India, Finland seek to deepen economic ties through startup cooperation: Envoy Mikko Kivikoski
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: "We want to engage more with the Indian startup actors. And here we see the startup sector, startup ecosystems, as an important part of that cooperation," Mikki Kivikoski said

“India and Finland are looking to deepen economic cooperation by strengthening ties between their startup ecosystems and promoting greater two-way investment,” Finnish Ambassador to India Mikko Kivikoski has said.

"We want to engage more with the Indian startup actors. And of course, at the end of the day, this is all about advancing the economic cooperation between our countries. And here we see the startup sector, startup ecosystems, as an important part of that cooperation," Mr. Kivikoski told PTI .

The Ambassador was speaking at an unconventional startup event held at the Embassy of Finland in New Delhi on Friday (November 20, 2026), where entrepreneurs stepped into an ice-cold pool to pitch their ideas, drawing on Finland's winter-swimming tradition. "We have quite a long tradition in Finland for these kinds of events," Mr. Kivikoski said.

"This year has been record-high when it comes to interaction and engagement between Finland and India," he said, referring to visits by the Finnish Prime Minister and President, as well as meetings between the leaders of the two countries.

The Ambassador said the two sides agreed to elevate their bilateral relationship to a Strategic Partnership in Digitalisation and Sustainability during Finnish President Alexander Stubb's state visit to India in March.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi met his Finnish counterpart, Petteri Orpo, in New Delhi on the sidelines of the AI Impact Summit in February and in Oslo on the margins of the 3rd India-Nordic Summit in May.

Mr. Kivikoski also referred to the visits to Finland by India's External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal during the summer. "We see India as a trusted partner when it comes to the Indo-Pacific area," he said.
The Ambassador said the India-Finland relationship was increasingly moving beyond conventional trade towards a partnership involving investments and people-to-people exchanges.

"What we are seeing already, and what is happening between the European Union and India and between India and Finland, is that we are now talking about partnership. It's not anymore about me selling something to you and you selling something to me," he said.

"There are more and more Finnish companies coming to the Indian market and more and more Indian companies going to the Finnish market. And of course we hope, and we are confident, that this dynamism will continue in the future," he said.

articles.title: Infra push and low base effect pushes core sector growth to series-high of 10.9% in October 2026
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: While the coal and electricity sectors saw growth shoot up, a large part of this was due to a statistical effect rather than growth in actual output. On the other hand, fuel-related sectors contracted again

Growth in the core industrial sectors of the economy climbed to a series-high of 10.9% in October 2026, driven by a surge in electricity generation, and coal, cement, and iron ore production, and a low base effect, official data released on Friday (November 20, 2026) showed.

Data released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on the Index of Core Industries shows that growth in October surpassed the 8.2% in September, the previous series high. The new index, released this year with a base year of 2022-23, has data that goes back only up to April 2024.
However, the data also shows that the strong growth figure in October was also likely aided by the fact that the index grew a relatively poor 0.8% in October last year.

“While core output surged by 10.9% in October 2026, the fastest pace in the new series, this was supported by a low base related to the shift in the festive calendar, with output having expanded by a marginal 0.8% in the year ago month,” Aditi Nayar, chief economist at ICRA said.

“While the growth print for October 2026 signals a strong start for the third quarter of FY2027, this is largely optical,” Ms. Nayar added. “The average performance for October-November 2026 would provide a better assessment, as this would adjust for festive base effects.”

Within the index, the coal sector saw growth accelerating to 23.05% in October 2026, far faster than the 10.7% registered in September. October’s performance, however, is likely also due to low base effect, since the sector contracted 8.4% in October last year.

The growth in the index, however, is in line with what the industry itself has reported. Coal India, the country’s largest coal company, reported that production increased about 19% to 67.2 million tonnes (MT) in October.

A major reason for the growth in coal production was likely demand from the power sector, which saw electricity generation jump by 21.6% in October 2026, up from 12.6% in the previous month. However, this sector too could have benefited from a low base effect, since it contracted nearly 7% in October 2025.
Within the index, the infrastructure-related sectors were the only ones that grew strongly without the aid of a statistical low base effect.

The iron ore sector, for example, grew at a three-month high of 23.4% in October 2026, compared to 18.4% in September and 8.7% in October last year. One of the factors driving this strong growth was that steel production grew at 7.3% in October, the fastest rate in seven months.

articles.title: CEA flags need to align capital markets with India’s development priorities
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Equity market capitalisation stood at around 130% of GDP, while the corporate bond market accounted for only about 16%.

Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran has called for a greater role for Indian capital markets in channelising household savings into productive investments, stressing the importance of patient capital in meeting the country’s long-term development needs.

Speaking at the CII Financial Summit in Mumbai, Mr. Nageswaran said sectors such as infrastructure, manufacturing, agriculture and mineral exploration required long-term financing, given their extended investment horizons.
Highlighting the imbalance in India’s financial markets, he pointed out that equity market capitalisation stood at around 130% of GDP, while the corporate bond market accounted for only about 16%.

While acknowledging that technology had improved market access, settlement systems and transaction security, he said these advances had not necessarily translated into better outcomes for investors or the real economy.

“A safer machine is not the same as a better outcome,” he said, emphasising that technological innovation should ultimately strengthen the capital market’s core function of converting savings into productive investments.
Cautioning against a consumption-led economic model, Mr. Nageswaran said, “An economy that is consumption-oriented may not be the most suited one for India’s development context.”

Echoing the need to promote long-term savings, Gaurav Mathur, founder and managing director of SafeGold, called for tax incentives to encourage investors to hold financial assets for longer periods. He stressed that savings policies should reflect individuals’ financial circumstances and different stages of life.

“It’s a matter of constructive partnership between regulators and financial intermediaries, where you incentivise long-term saving behaviour at the appropriate stages in life,” Mr. Mathur said, adding that incentives should particularly target wealthier individuals with greater capacity to save.

Meanwhile, Nilesh Shah, managing director of Kotak Mahindra Asset Management Company and part-time member of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister, underscored the need to strengthen financial literacy and encourage voluntary pension savings. He said these measures were increasingly important amid uncertainties over employment and income in a technology-driven economy.

articles.title: How AI could reshape global growth and productivity
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: A key expected impact of AI is an unprecedented rise in labour productivity, as its success as a technological revolution is premised on such an increase; what remains to be seen is how pervasive its impact will be across different sectors of the economy

Many have likened the artificial intelligence (AI) phenomenon to the inventions of the steam engine or internal combustion engine in the 18th and 19th centuries, respectively. Only time can tell whether AI is epochal of that kind. In this two-part piece, we discuss the possible impact it may have on the global economy as a whole.

A key impact of AI is considered to be an unprecedented rise in labour productivity. In fact, if there is one purpose AI is supposed to serve, it is enhancing labour productivity multifold. Since labour productivity is a key variable in this puzzle, consider what it constitutes of (Box 1) . It is a ratio of output and workers employed. Now this ratio can rise in three different ways — a rise in output for a given number of workers employed (rise in the numerator); a loss of jobs which leads to a fall in the denominator; more jobs are created, but the output rises faster than the jobs (while both the numerator and the denominator are rising, the numerator rises faster than the denominator).

There is usually a distinction drawn between a case where there is a net loss of jobs versus one where jobs grow, but the output grows even faster. The latter is preferred over the former. Even though AI may displace white-collar workers, it may generate more jobs for the blue-collar workers, so in the net there may not be a job loss with AI adoption across the economy. However, for the argument we make below, it does not matter which of the three sources leads to a rise in productivity. Why should the rise in labour productivity matter? There are two contrasting takes on this question in the economics discipline.

One which argues that productivity growth increases the growth of output in the economy. The idea is simple. Growth of output is a function of its two inputs — labour and capital. Since capital enhances the productivity of labour, the rate at which output can grow is the sum of the growth of the labour force and its productivity. So, if the workforce grows at 2% and productivity at 4%, the economy would stabilise at 6% growth over time. And if the rate of labour productivity rises, according to this framework, growth in the economy rises pari passu (Graph 1a).

Between the three variables — output growth, labour growth and productivity growth — output growth adjusts to the other two. This is what Robert Solow, a celebrated economist and a Nobel laureate, showed in a seminal paper on growth theory. What he did not explain though was why and where did this labour productivity rise come from. Much later, his successors argued that the growth of labour productivity depends on investment in human capital, research and development, patent regimes, etc., what came to be known as endogenous growth theories.

A key expected impact of AI is an unprecedented rise in labour productivity, as its success as a technological revolution is premised on such an increase; what remains to be seen is how pervasive its impact will be across different sectors of the economy

Many have likened the artificial intelligence (AI) phenomenon to the inventions of the steam engine or internal combustion engine in the 18th and 19th centuries, respectively. Only time can tell whether AI is epochal of that kind. In this two-part piece, we discuss the possible impact it may have on the global economy as a whole.

A key impact of AI is considered to be an unprecedented rise in labour productivity. In fact, if there is one purpose AI is supposed to serve, it is enhancing labour productivity multifold. Since labour productivity is a key variable in this puzzle, consider what it constitutes of (Box 1) . It is a ratio of output and workers employed. Now this ratio can rise in three different ways — a rise in output for a given number of workers employed (rise in the numerator); a loss of jobs which leads to a fall in the denominator; more jobs are created, but the output rises faster than the jobs (while both the numerator and the denominator are rising, the numerator rises faster than the denominator).

There is usually a distinction drawn between a case where there is a net loss of jobs versus one where jobs grow, but the output grows even faster. The latter is preferred over the former. Even though AI may displace white-collar workers, it may generate more jobs for the blue-collar workers, so in the net there may not be a job loss with AI adoption across the economy. However, for the argument we make below, it does not matter which of the three sources leads to a rise in productivity. Why should the rise in labour productivity matter? There are two contrasting takes on this question in the economics discipline.

One which argues that productivity growth increases the growth of output in the economy. The idea is simple. Growth of output is a function of its two inputs — labour and capital. Since capital enhances the productivity of labour, the rate at which output can grow is the sum of the growth of the labour force and its productivity. So, if the workforce grows at 2% and productivity at 4%, the economy would stabilise at 6% growth over time. And if the rate of labour productivity rises, according to this framework, growth in the economy rises pari passu (Graph 1a).

Between the three variables — output growth, labour growth and productivity growth — output growth adjusts to the other two. This is what Robert Solow, a celebrated economist and a Nobel laureate, showed in a seminal paper on growth theory. What he did not explain though was why and where did this labour productivity rise come from. Much later, his successors argued that the growth of labour productivity depends on investment in human capital, research and development, patent regimes, etc., what came to be known as endogenous growth theories.

articles.title: Immigration officers make arrest at Seattle airport in ‘distressing’ scene, delaying flight
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred"

Masked immigration officers detained at least one person on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday (November 22, 2026) as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.
Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.
Alaska Airlines said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognise how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."
It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect".
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities".

articles.title: Bahrain says Iran struck industrial site as tankers hit in Hormuz
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: “Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said
Bahrain accused Iran of striking a civilian industrial facility on Saturday (November 21, 2026), causing a fire and damage but no casualties, while two tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz.

"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site. Civil Defence is working to bring the fire under control," the Interior Ministry said on X, without specifying the location.
Residents told AFP they saw smoke rising over Sitra Island, on Bahrain's east coast, home to several industrial sites including a refinery run by state oil company Bapco.
Iran's Fars news agency reported the Revolutionary Guards had "attacked two U.S. bases, Sheikh Isa and Juffair, on the island of Bahrain in response to the illegal actions of the United States".

The attacks came as two tankers were struck in the Strait of Hormuz, which has become the focus of the stalemated conflict, with Iran continuing in its efforts to blockade the strategic shipping line.
The U.S. military, meanwhile, has been escorting ships through the strategic strait, which carried one-fifth of the world's oil before the war, and maintains its own counterblockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday (November 21, 2026) that a Qatari delegation visited Tehran the previous evening and "held two hours of talks", without providing details.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said: "The ongoing talks in the region must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally."
"Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless," he said, quoted by state TV.
Iran's demands include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the U.S. counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

While addressing the press after the November 19 summit with American and Chinese leaders in Shenzhen, the Chinese tech hub, Russian President Vladimir Putin responded to comparisons between the trilateral and the 1945 Yalta Conference . “What was wrong with Yalta? What was so bad about it?” he said, while responding to a question. “At Yalta, the victory over Nazism was codified... I wouldn’t mind — in fact, I would consider it right — to codify a victory over ‘neo-Nazism’ as well,” Mr. Putin said.

At the Yalta Conference, one of the most consequential diplomatic summits of the 20th century, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, American President Franklin D. Roosevelt, and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill assembled in the Crimean city to discuss the post-war political order. In February 1945, when the summit was held, the Soviet Red Army had pushed deep into Eastern Europe and was marching towards Berlin while the Allied forces were advancing from Western Europe. The defeat of Nazi Germany was certain. The leaders decided that Germany would be divided, German militarism would be eliminated, and Nazi institutions would be dismantled. The summit played an important role in shaping the post-war European order.
Global & Diplomatic Brief: The Shenzhen trilateral | The unlikely trio. This development underscores India's strategic autonomy and pragmatic engagement in bilateral and multilateral diplomacy.

articles.title: The Rohingya | Vindication for a persecuted people
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The International Court of Justice’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide during its 2017 ‘clearance operations’ offers a measure of justice for the ethnic and religious minority, but the court has no means of enforcing its judgment

In a first of a kind ruling, the International Court of Justice held on November 19 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during the military’s “clearance operations” in 2017. This was the first time the ICJ found a state responsible for committing genocide. Nine judges against six voted in favour of the ruling, in a case brought in 2019 by The Gambia.

The court also found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by civilians who joined its forces, failed to punish the perpetrators, never enacted the laws that the Genocide Convention requires, and destroyed evidence in breach of the court’s 2020 interim order. It also rejected, by 14 votes to one, the charge that Myanmar directly and publicly incited private persons to commit genocide, but declined to order citizenship for the Rohingya.

The judgment holds the state of Myanmar to account but does not convict any individual. It is final and cannot be appealed. The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and, if warranted, prosecute those responsible, guarantee that the violations will not recur, allow the “safe, voluntary and dignified” return of the displaced, restore their property and compensate the Rohingya. The amount of compensation is to be fixed later, after Myanmar reports back to the court within two years.

The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim people who speak an Indo-Aryan language close to the Chittagonian dialect. The 2014 Census in Myanmar estimated over a million Rohingya in the country, concentrated in Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung along the Bangladesh border. Muslims have lived in Rakhine or Arakan from the time of the Mrauk U kingdom (15th to 18th century). In 1799, the British physician Francis Buchanan recorded that Muslims “long settled in Arakan” called themselves the “Rooinga”.

Many joined them, coming from Chittagong during colonial rule. Historian Jacques Leider has said the “Rohingya” took on a political and ethnic meaning in the late 1950s, when Muslim leaders adopted it to claim the status of a “national race”. In 1961, Brig. Aung Gyi of the Burmese Army publicly accepted them as an ethnic group. But this was before the coup by General Ne Win in 1962 which heralded decades of rule by the military junta in the country.

📰 The Rohingya | Vindication for a persecuted people

🎯 Exam Relevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

The International Court of Justice’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide during its 2017 ‘clearance operations’ offers a measure of justice for the ethnic and religious minority, but the court has no means of enforcing its judgment

In a first of a kind ruling, the International Court of Justice held on November 19 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during the military’s “clearance operations” in 2017. This was the first time the ICJ found a state responsible for committing genocide. Nine judges against six voted in favour of the ruling, in a case brought in 2019 by The Gambia.

The court also found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by civilians who joined its forces, failed to punish the perpetrators, never enacted the laws that the Genocide Convention requires, and destroyed evidence in breach of the court’s 2020 interim order. It also rejected, by 14 votes to one, the charge that Myanmar directly and publicly incited private persons to commit genocide, but declined to order citizenship for the Rohingya.

The judgment holds the state of Myanmar to account but does not convict any individual. It is final and cannot be appealed. The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and, if warranted, prosecute those responsible, guarantee that the violations will not recur, allow the “safe, voluntary and dignified” return of the displaced, restore their property and compensate the Rohingya. The amount of compensation is to be fixed later, after Myanmar reports back to the court within two years.

The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim people who speak an Indo-Aryan language close to the Chittagonian dialect. The 2014 Census in Myanmar estimated over a million Rohingya in the country, concentrated in Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung along the Bangladesh border. Muslims have lived in Rakhine or Arakan from the time of the Mrauk U kingdom (15th to 18th century). In 1799, the British physician Francis Buchanan recorded that Muslims “long settled in Arakan” called themselves the “Rooinga”.

Many joined them, coming from Chittagong during colonial rule. Historian Jacques Leider has said the “Rohingya” took on a political and ethnic meaning in the late 1950s, when Muslim leaders adopted it to claim the status of a “national race”. In 1961, Brig. Aung Gyi of the Burmese Army publicly accepted them as an ethnic group. But this was before the coup by General Ne Win in 1962 which heralded decades of rule by the military junta in the country.

fullParagraphs: The ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is significant, but refugees continue to face the threat of violence and restrictions on humanitarian access, as the situation in their homeland remains precarious

T he International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN’s top court, on November 19, ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority during the military’s 2017 clearance operations in Rakhine State. This was the first time the world court held a country responsible for committing genocide.

The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority, have faced decades of systematic discrimination in the Southeast Asian country, including the denial of citizenship, restrictions on movement and access to education, healthcare and livelihoods.

In August 2017, a military crackdown involving mass killings, sexual violence, and the burning of villages forced more than 7,40,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh. They joined earlier waves of refugees who had escaped persecution. Nearly 1.2 million Rohingya now live in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar. Rohingya refugees in other countries such as India, Malaysia and Indonesia also face uncertain legal status, discrimination, detention and the threat of deportation.
Meanwhile, their homeland remains deeply troubled. Rakhine State has been engulfed in fighting between Myanmar’s military and the Arakan Army, a rebel group which now controls much of the region.

The Rohingya, many of whom remain internally displaced, face renewed insecurity, restrictions on humanitarian access and the threat of violence from competing armed forces. And for the refugees, a return to their homeland is neither desirable nor practical. While the ICJ verdict is significant and sets a strong precedent, it is unlikely to ease the suffering of the Rohingya.

articles.title: How U.S. controls flow of advanced tech, chip, and compute to China | Explained
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The U.S. Commerce Department on November 16 issued an interim final rule barring data centre operators outside the U.S. equipped with advanced American AI chips from providing cloud service to businesses in two dozen countries, including China, Iran, and Russia

The story so far: The battle for the most-sought-after commodity that underpins development of artificial intelligence technology just grew fiercer. On November 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim final rule (IFR) requiring companies to have licences to supply advanced American AI chips to data centre operators outside the U.S. with substantial computing power to businesses headquartered in two dozen countries, including China, Iran, and Russia. The new rule restricts American companies from freely shipping high-end AI chips to a set of five countries, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore, without the explicit approval of the U.S. government.

China has censured the move, calling it “yet another case of the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing export control measures to interfere in normal trade and tech cooperation between China and other countries and go after China’s high-tech industry”. The interim rule came just days ahead of the meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China on the sidelines of the November 18-19 APEC Summit.

The U.S. government’s policy on making advanced technology inaccessible to China has been a talking point among lawmakers in Washington for well over a decade, but Congress strengthened the extant legal framework only during the first Trump term when it passed the Export Control Reform Act in 2018.

It strengthened the U.S. government’s authority to control the movement of advanced technology originating in the country, and included curbing exports of sensitive technologies, including top-tier chips, with dual-use — both commercial and military — applications to countries such as China, Russia, and Iran.

A year later, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) placed Chinese telecom equipment maker Huawei and its affiliates on the Entity List, effectively blocking their access to high-end semiconductors.

fullParagraphs: Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early
The craze for fairness is more than skin-deep, and the trade-off can be costly. Inferior cosmetic products can end up harming your vital organs.

A 17-year-old girl in Keralam’s Malappuram developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, according to the doctors treating her.

The incident came to light after the authorities at the hospital that treated the teenager, who was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, held a press conference on Friday. Lab tests had confirmed 1.25% mercury in the cosmetic product, according to the hospital sources.

Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early.

Warning against following social media beauty trends and using topical creams seen online or bought over the counter without a prescription, M.M. Faizal, former president of the Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists, says people lack awareness of how topical applications can enter the bloodstream.

“People are obsessed with fair skin. We have observed a rise in the number of people buying steroid creams that are easily available over the counter and applying them to their faces. Such steroid-based applications and creams containing heavy metals such as mercury can damage your kidneys easily. The government needs to bring in some mechanisms to control this,” he says.

A rise in the number of teenagers relying on spurious beauty products has forced the Keralam Drugs Control department to launch awareness campaigns targeting students in Classes XI and XII, an age group particularly vulnerable to online campaigns. Frequent inspections are carried out in marketplaces to confiscate spurious cosmetics.
State Drugs Controller K. Sujith Kumar says raising awareness about such spurious cosmetic products is the only way forward.
“We have seized cosmetics that have high mercury levels from offline markets. But there is no way to track or regulate online marketplaces,” he says.

Prolonged use of such creams can lead to kidney damage, says former secretary of the Nephrology Association of Kerala, Jayant Thomas Mathew, who has come across a few cases of kidney disorders among users. The condition could be detected early because the patients were aware of the symptoms.

articles.title: COP31 extends into overtime in Turkiye meeting
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The inability to reach compromise — every clause of the final text must be agreed upon by every participant country — is due to the familiar division between a bloc of European countries, and developing countries over a timeline to phase out fossil fuels

Much like the 1.5 degree Celsius warming ceiling, COP31 proceedings under way at Antalya in Turkiye also breached upper limits with countries, as of Saturday (November 21, 2026) evening, yet to behold a final text or convene a final plenary meeting to decide on the path forward for climate action.

Proceedings were expected to officially conclude on Friday (November 20, 2026), though historically it almost always goes into overtime and extends into the early hours of the weekend. The inability to reach a compromise — every clause of the final text must be agreed upon by every participating country — is due to the familiar division between a bloc of European countries and developing countries over a timeline to phase out fossil fuels and defining and paying out the trillions of dollars necessary to fund that transition as well as adapt to ongoing climate change.

The latest public iteration of the COP31 draft cover text, as of November 19, has eliminated references to fossil fuels phase out and net zero dates but has also deleted references to a firm US $120 billion adaptation-finance target that developing countries have been asking for as “legally binding financial obligations” on developed countries.

Taking off from the previous editions of the COP in Baku, Azerbaijan and Belem, Brazil, developed nations said they would “take the lead” in contributing at least $300 billion annually towards mitigation and adaptation to climate change by 2035, though developing countries say this should be at least $ 1.3 trillion.

Other than the thorny debate on whether loans, grants, and for-profit investments in green projects are all included in this number, there is also debate on how much of the annual money should be split between adaptation and mitigation. The $120 billion was a proposal but that now has disappeared from the latest version of the text.
This suggests that the most ambitious demands of both the developed and developing country blocs have been eliminated.

A cover text is an overarching political decision that frames the outcome of a climate conference rather than settling any single agenda item. It is usually finalised last, and like every outcome it needs the consensus of all Parties. The Presidency has said earlier drafts were not meant to reflect consensus.

However, a widely expected outcome of raising electricity’s share in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 and scaling up the use of carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) technologies. The latter involves unproven, expensive technology to extract atmospheric carbon dioxide. Proponents say this is necessary to counter the effects of the carbon that’s already in the atmosphere and responsible for the 1.5C temperature breach that has already occurred. To reiterate, the Paris Agreement goal is to keep temperatures below 2C and “as far as possible” below 1.5C. However, this has also been criticised by several civil society organisations as being an excuse to delay fossil-fuel phaseout.

“CC[U]S has been researched and developed for decades yet has achieved no discernible breakthroughs in efficiency, capture rates, or costs. Indeed, costs are getting higher. CCS is a tax on energy supplies at a time when affordability is strained and demand growth is seeking efficient supplies,” said Grant Hauber, Strategic Energy Finance Advisor, Asia, Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) in a statement,” CO2 capture and disposal are a pure cost to the energy and production system.”

“We’re down to the wire at COP31, and the latest texts are alarmingly far from ambitious or equitable,” said Rachel Cleetus, Climate Program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS), in a statement. “ Rich nations, most notably the EU nations, are still holding a harsh line against committing to tripling adaptation finance to at least $120 billion annually by 2035. Instead of reaching agreement on urgently needed climate finance, some countries seem willing to push negotiations toward failure.”

fullParagraphs: Nearly 87% of its annual target cohort of 14-year-old girls has been covered under the national cervical cancer prevention campaign. Uttar Pradesh leads with more than 29.33 lakh girls vaccinated, followed by Bihar (13.70 lakh) and Gujarat (7.75 lakh)

India has administered more than one crore doses of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine in less than nine months, covering nearly 87% of its annual target cohort of 14-year-old girls under the national cervical cancer prevention campaign launched in February 2026, noted a release issued by the Union Health Ministry on Saturday (November 21, 2026).

It added that Uttar Pradesh leads with more than 29.33 lakh girls vaccinated, followed by Bihar (13.70 lakh) and Gujarat (7.75 lakh). Six States — Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Mizoram, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar — have achieved 100% coverage of their identified target populations.

The government provides the single-dose vaccine free of cost and voluntarily to eligible girls at designated government health facilities, with parental consent. The U-WIN digital platform facilitates beneficiary tracking, real-time monitoring, slot booking and digital certificates. Vaccination sessions are conducted under medical supervision, with arrangements for managing adverse events following immunisation, the Ministry said.
Among other high-performing States, Assam has recorded 95.63% coverage, followed by Telangana (95.28%), Karnataka (93.16%) and Uttarakhand (90.17%).

Chhattisgarh (86.21%) and Rajasthan (85.23%) have crossed the 80% coverage mark, while Kerala (77.02%), Tamil Nadu (76.12%), Odisha (74.90%) and the Union Territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (72.99%) have achieved more than 70% coverage.

In terms of absolute numbers, Uttar Pradesh leads the country with more than 29.33 lakh 14-year-old girls vaccinated, followed by Bihar with more than 13.70 lakh and Gujarat with more than 7.75 lakh girls vaccinated.

“School teachers, Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs) and other frontline healthcare workers have worked closely with parents and communities to encourage informed participation and counter misinformation,’’ the Ministry added.

It stated that digital health infrastructure has been an important enabler of the nationwide campaign, with the U-WIN platform supporting real-time monitoring, beneficiary tracking and digital vaccination records.

The platform also enables parents to book HPV vaccination slots for their daughters and download digital vaccination certificates, making the vaccination process more accessible, convenient and transparent.
